newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesians not worried about U.S. campaign row.
newsitem.headline: Indonesians not worried about U.S. campaign row.

text.p: Businessmen here said on Friday they were not worried about a row in the U.S. presidential campaign over contributions to the Democratic Party by Indonesians as it was unlikely to affect bilateral trade.
"I don't think the issue will have any impact on our exports to the United States," Petrus A. Patinama, executive director of the Indonesian Footwear Association, told Reuters.
He said the United States accounted for 52 percent of Indonesia's footwear exports, which totalled $2.05 billion in overall value in 1995.
Business leaders and diplomats tended to dismiss the funding row as U.S. election politics which would likely blow over after the November vote.

U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich on Thursday called for an investigation into whether Indonesia won U.S. foreign policy favours in return for contributions from individuals connected to the Indonesian Lippo Group to the Democratic Party.
The Clinton administration has said Indonesia had not received any favourable treatment.
"I don't think such a case will affect our exports to the United States," the Jakarta Post newspaper quoted Gemala Group Chairman Sofyan Wanandi as saying.

"We know that many businessmen there are supporters of the Republican Party, but they won't blow the issue out of proportion and involve the economy," said Winandi, whose group has interests in property, trading and pharmaceutical products.
Patinama said Indonesia's footwear companies did not have any problem in penetrating the U.S. market and had not faced any quotas on its export.

He said Indonesian footwear manufacturers were often under close scrutiny from the American public particularly over workers' treatment as reflected by a recent visit by human rights campaigner Jesse Jackson.
He said the association had not lobbied the U.S. administration over its treatment of workers, saying it was not necessary. He said improving the lot of the workers was more important than lobbying.
Nike Inc and Reebok International Ltd source a substantial quantity of their products from Indonesia.
A senior Asian diplomat described the issue as "election politics". He said the Clinton administration appeared quite confident about handling the row.
"At the moment I don't think it is having very much of an impact on relations between the two countries," he said.
